sql_code: SELECT *
FROM network_latency
LIMIT 100
-- reps_per_arm replaces a separate failures query. That query reported the
-- repetitions the runner caught failing -- two, both on GCP -- and neither
-- cost a measurement: the affected arms ended with the same repetition count
-- as their siblings. It therefore invited a reader to infer lost data where
-- there was none, while not answering whether coverage is actually even.
-- This does answer it. latency_rows / arms is repetitions per arm: a whole
-- number means every arm in the group was measured the same number of times,
-- and a fraction means at least one is short.
SELECT provider,
placement_class,
os_tuning,
count(DISTINCT benchmark_name)                    AS arms,
count(*)                                          AS latency_rows,
round(count(*) * 1.0 / nullif(count(DISTINCT benchmark_name), 0), 1) AS reps_per_arm,
round(min(p50_rtt_us) / 1000.0, 3)                AS best_p50_ms,
round(max(p99_rtt_us) / 1000.0, 1)                AS worst_p99_ms
FROM network_latency
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
ORDER BY 1, 2, 3

description: UDP tail advantage by placement and offered rate
sql_code: -- The headline. Positive advantage means UDP's 99th percentile is lower.
-- TCP and UDP move a packet identically; the difference appears only where
-- TCP's control loop engages, and how hard it engages scales with RTT.
-- Grouped by provider on purpose. Pooling them mixes STACKIT's packet-rate
-- ceiling -- which caps UDP at ~60k packets/s and is a property of its NIC, not
-- of the transport -- into the same row as providers that have no such limit,
-- and the average then says nothing true about either.
SELECT provider,
placement_class,
offered_mps,
round(median(CASE WHEN protocol = 'tcp' THEN p99_rtt_us END) / 1000.0, 2) AS tcp_p99_ms,
round(median(CASE WHEN protocol = 'udp' THEN p99_rtt_us END) / 1000.0, 2) AS udp_p99_ms,
round(median(CASE WHEN protocol = 'tcp' THEN p99_rtt_us END)
/ nullif(median(CASE WHEN protocol = 'udp' THEN p99_rtt_us END), 0), 1) AS udp_advantage_x,
-- Contention, on the same row as the numbers it may explain. NULL means
-- the run has no CPU telemetry, not that the host was quiet.
round(avg(worst_steal_pct), 1)            AS steal_pct
FROM network_latency
WHERE mode = 'ul'
-- Standard tuning only. STACKIT is the one provider that also ran a tuned
-- arm, so pooling the two would mix treatments -- and those runs happened to
-- draw quieter hosts, which biases pooled STACKIT figures optimistically:
-- at 100k UDP the tuned rows read 81.3% delivered against standard's 44.1%.
AND os_tuning = 'standard'
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
ORDER BY 1, 2, 3

placement_class,
offered_mps,
round(median(delivered_pct), 3)                  AS udp_delivered_pct,

-- the run has no CPU telemetry, not that the host was quiet.
round(avg(worst_steal_pct), 1)            AS steal_pct
FROM network_latency
WHERE mode = 'ul'
AND protocol = 'udp'
-- Standard tuning only. STACKIT is the one provider that also ran a tuned
-- arm, so pooling the two would mix treatments -- and those runs happened to
-- draw quieter hosts, which biases pooled STACKIT figures optimistically:
-- at 100k UDP the tuned rows read 81.3% delivered against standard's 44.1%.
AND os_tuning = 'standard'
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3

FROM network_latency
WHERE mode = 'ul'
-- Standard tuning only. STACKIT is the one provider that also ran a tuned
-- arm, so pooling the two would mix treatments -- and those runs happened to
-- draw quieter hosts, which biases pooled STACKIT figures optimistically:
-- at 100k UDP the tuned rows read 81.3% delivered against standard's 44.1%.
AND os_tuning = 'standard'
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3, 4

sql_code: -- The closed-loop half of this study, and the floor everything else is read
-- against.
-- sockperf ping-pong keeps exactly one message in flight: the sender waits for
-- each reply before sending again, so offered load is whatever the round trip
-- allows and no queue can build. The other latency queries in this group are
-- open loop -- sockperf under-load emits at a fixed rate regardless of what
-- comes back -- which is the only way to see what happens when a receiver
-- falls behind, and also the only way to build a queue that shows up as
-- latency. Comparing the two operating points is what the coordinated-omission
-- query in Measurement Validity does.
-- So this is the transport cost with the queueing removed: near enough pure
-- distance, serialisation and stack traversal. Measured medians run 170 us
-- intra-AZ, 467 us multi-AZ and 66,900 us cross-region -- a spread of about
-- 390x, not the three orders of magnitude an earlier version of this comment
-- claimed.
-- The consequence for reading the rest: a protocol difference of tens of
-- microseconds is decisive intra-AZ and invisible cross-region, so the
-- comparison has to be made inside a placement and never across one.
SELECT provider,
placement_class,
protocol,
round(median(p50_rtt_us), 1) AS p50_us,
round(median(p99_rtt_us), 1) AS p99_us,
-- Contention, on the same row as the numbers it may explain. NULL means
-- the run has no CPU telemetry, not that the host was quiet.
round(avg(worst_steal_pct), 1)            AS steal_pct
FROM network_latency
WHERE mode = 'pp'
-- Standard tuning only. STACKIT is the one provider that also ran a tuned
-- arm, so pooling the two would mix treatments -- and those runs happened to
-- draw quieter hosts, which biases pooled STACKIT figures optimistically:
-- at 100k UDP the tuned rows read 81.3% delivered against standard's 44.1%.
AND os_tuning = 'standard'
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
ORDER BY 1, 2, 3

geom_col(position = "dodge") +
facet_wrap(~ provider) +
scale_y_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
labs(x = "Placement", y = "Ping-pong p50 RTT (us, log scale)", fill = "Protocol") +
theme_bw() +
theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
plot(output); dev.off(); to_svg() # output to the html page

description: Effect of the network-throughput tuning profile
sql_code: -- Only STACKIT was run with both profiles. The profile changes three things at
-- once (congestion control, qdisc, socket buffers), so a difference here cannot
-- be attributed to any one of them.
SELECT os_tuning,
protocol,
offered_mps,
round(median(p50_rtt_us), 1) AS p50_us,
round(median(p99_rtt_us), 1) AS p99_us,
any_value(tuning_congestion_control) AS congestion_control,
any_value(tuning_rmem_max)           AS rmem_max,
-- Contention, on the same row as the numbers it may explain. NULL means
-- the run has no CPU telemetry, not that the host was quiet.
round(avg(worst_steal_pct), 1)            AS steal_pct
FROM network_latency
WHERE mode = 'ul'
AND provider = 'stackit'
AND placement_class = 'different-host-single-az'
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
ORDER BY 3, 1, 2

description: Hypervisor CPU steal, and which rows it invalidates
sql_code: -- The covariate to check before reading any STACKIT number in this study.
-- AWS and GCP measured 0.0% mean steal on the benchmark core across every run
-- ever made here, peaking at 4.3% on a single AWS repetition and 0.0% on GCP,
-- and neither exceeded 5% in any repetition. STACKIT averaged 10.1% mean,
-- exceeded 5% in 56% of its repetitions, and peaked at 74.0%. Counted per
-- provisioning rather than per repetition, taking the worse of the two ends,
-- 12 of 14 STACKIT provisionings were contended against 0 of 9 on AWS and 0
-- of 6 on GCP -- so contention is the normal case there, not the exception,
-- and there is no practical retry-until-quiet strategy. That is a product
-- difference, not a network-stack one, but it lands on the same measurement.
-- Why it matters more than it looks. sockperf under-load has the server echo
-- every message, so a descheduled server vCPU sits directly inside the
-- round-trip time being reported. A contended STACKIT run and a genuine
-- transport effect are indistinguishable in the latency column alone.
-- This was found by hand after a busy_poll arm appeared to deliver a 4x
-- improvement that turned out to be its control sitting on a host with 31%
-- steal against the treatment's 0.7%. Treat any comparison whose two sides
-- differ by more than a few points of steal as uninterpretable.
SELECT c.provider,
c.client_machine_type,
cpu.role,
count(*)                                            AS cpu_rows,
round(avg(cpu.steal_pct), 1)                        AS steal_pct_mean,
round(max(cpu.steal_pct_max), 1)                    AS steal_pct_peak,
round(100.0 * avg(case when cpu.steal_pct > 5
then 1 else 0 end), 0)       AS pct_rows_over_5
FROM network_cpu cpu
JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT run_id, scenario_name, provider, client_machine_type
FROM network_latency) c
ON c.run_id = cpu.run_id AND c.scenario_name = cpu.scenario_name
-- CPU 1 is the benchmark core: remote_cpu_list() pins benchmarks to 1..n-1
-- and leaves CPU 0 for the telemetry samplers.
WHERE cpu.cpu = 1
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
ORDER BY steal_pct_mean DESC
r_code: to_svg <- svgstring(width = output.width.inch, height = output.height.inch, scaling = 1)
### the current table is bound to the variable 'df'
output <- ggplot(df, aes(x = provider, y = steal_pct_mean, fill = role)) +
geom_col(position = "dodge") +
geom_text(aes(label = round(steal_pct_mean, 1)),
position = position_dodge(width = 0.9), vjust = -0.4, size = 3) +
geom_hline(yintercept = 5, linetype = "dashed") +
labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean %steal on the benchmark core", fill = "Host",
title = "Hypervisor contention by provider",
subtitle = "Dashed line is the 5% admission threshold. AWS and GCP sit at zero.") +
theme_bw()
plot(output); dev.off(); to_svg() # output to the html page

description: Was UDP loss buffer limited? (socket fill against offered rate)
sql_code: -- The socket receive buffer, read out of ss rather than inferred from a
-- sysctl. rb_bytes is what the socket actually got; queue_fill_ratio is how
-- close the receive queue came to filling it.
-- Measured server side, UDP, across every run: fill climbs 0.004 at
-- ping-pong to 0.568 at 100k msg/s, and drops appear exactly where fill
-- starts rising -- 0 below 10k, 36 at 10k, 347,416 at 100k. That is a
-- buffer-limited system, and nstat agrees: every loss is UdpRcvbufErrors
-- with IpInDiscards at zero, so nothing was lost in the network.
-- The catch, and the reason this query exists. rb_bytes was 212992 in all
-- 561 socket samples on record, in every arm -- including the
-- network-throughput arm, which raises net.core.rmem_max 630x to
-- 134217728. rmem_max only caps what an application may request, and UDP
-- has no receive autotuning, so the socket took rmem_default and the
-- profile never touched it. The study's conclusion that a 630x buffer did
-- not reduce UDP loss was drawn from a buffer that never changed.
-- Treat rb_bytes as the check that a buffer treatment took effect. The
-- kernel sets it to 2 * min(request, rmem_max), so a request above the
-- ceiling is silently clamped and the requested column will not show it.
SELECT s.provider,
sk.benchmark_name,
l.offered_mps,
round(avg(sk.rb_bytes))                        AS rb_bytes,
round(avg(sk.queue_fill_ratio), 3)             AS queue_fill_ratio,
round(avg(sk.drops_delta))                     AS socket_drops,
round(avg(l.delivered_pct), 1)                 AS delivered_pct
FROM network_socket sk
JOIN network_latency l
ON  l.run_id         = sk.run_id
AND l.scenario_name  = sk.scenario_name
AND l.benchmark_name = sk.benchmark_name
AND l.repetition     = sk.repetition
JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT run_id, scenario_name, provider FROM network_latency) s
ON s.run_id = sk.run_id AND s.scenario_name = sk.scenario_name
-- The receiving end is where a buffer overflows.
WHERE sk.role = 'server' AND l.protocol = 'udp'
-- Standard tuning only. STACKIT is the one provider that also ran a tuned
-- arm, so pooling the two would mix treatments -- and those runs happened to
-- draw quieter hosts, which biases pooled STACKIT figures optimistically:
-- at 100k UDP the tuned rows read 81.3% delivered against standard's 44.1%.
AND l.os_tuning = 'standard'
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
ORDER BY 1, 3
r_code: to_svg <- svgstring(width = output.width.inch, height = output.height.inch, scaling = 1)
### the current table is bound to the variable 'df'
### Ping-pong is excluded from the plot, explicitly rather than by letting
### ggplot drop it: it has one message in flight and so no offered rate, and
### its NA would vanish silently on a log axis. It stays in the table above
### as the zero-load baseline -- fill 0.003-0.004, zero drops.
output <- ggplot(subset(df, !is.na(offered_mps)), aes(x = offered_mps, y = queue_fill_ratio)) +
geom_line() +
geom_point(aes(size = socket_drops), alpha = 0.7) +
geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
facet_wrap(~ provider) +
scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
labs(x = "Offered rate (messages/s, log scale)",
y = "Receive queue depth / socket buffer", size = "Socket drops",
title = "Was UDP loss buffer limited?",
subtitle = "Drops appear as the queue approaches the buffer ceiling (dashed line).") +
theme_bw()
plot(output); dev.off(); to_svg() # output to the html page

description: How contention moves delivery (intra-AZ, by offered rate)
sql_code: -- One row per repetition, with placement held fixed and offered rate faceted,
-- because both of those move latency far more than contention does and an
-- earlier version of this query controlled for neither.
-- What that cost: pooled across placements, the AWS and GCP points span 110
-- to 1,113,963 us of p99 while sitting at exactly 0% steal, because
-- cross-region round trips are ~390x intra-AZ ones. That is placement
-- variance drawn on a contention axis, and it makes any apparent relationship
-- unattributable -- which is the objection this rewrite answers.
-- Fixing placement and rate also changed the claim. Within STACKIT
-- different-host at a single rung, contention predicts DELIVERY strongly and
-- consistently -- r = -0.65, -0.92, -0.76 for UDP at 25k, 50k and 100k msg/s
-- -- while its correlation with p99 is weak and unstable across the same
-- cells, running +0.64, +0.38, -0.05. So this query is about delivered rate.
-- Tail latency is still reported per row, but it is not what the controlled
-- data supports a claim about.
-- Read the two protocols against each other. TCP's delivered percentage has
-- zero variance here -- it is 100 in every repetition at every steal level,
-- which is why its correlation is undefined rather than weak. Its receive
-- window throttles the sender when the receiver stalls, so contention costs
-- it queueing rather than data. UDP has no such feedback and converts the
-- same stall into loss.
-- different-host-single-az is the one placement all three providers ran, so
-- fixing it here keeps the provider comparison intact.
SELECT provider,
protocol,
offered_mps,
round(worst_steal_pct, 1)      AS steal_pct,
round(delivered_pct, 1)        AS delivered_pct,
round(p99_rtt_us)              AS p99_us
FROM network_latency
WHERE mode = 'ul'
AND placement_class = 'different-host-single-az'
AND offered_mps >= 25000
-- NULL steal means the run predates CPU telemetry, not that it was quiet.
AND worst_steal_pct IS NOT NULL
-- Standard tuning only. STACKIT is the one provider that also ran a tuned
-- arm, so pooling the two would mix treatments -- and those runs happened to
-- draw quieter hosts, which biases pooled STACKIT figures optimistically:
-- at 100k UDP the tuned rows read 81.3% delivered against standard's 44.1%.
AND os_tuning = 'standard'
ORDER BY provider, protocol, offered_mps, steal_pct
r_code: to_svg <- svgstring(width = output.width.inch, height = output.height.inch, scaling = 1)
### the current table is bound to the variable 'df'
### Faceted by offered rate, not pooled: rate drives delivery on its own, so
### pooling the rungs would put the same confound back on the x axis.
output <- ggplot(df, aes(x = steal_pct, y = delivered_pct, colour = protocol, shape = provider)) +
geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1.8) +
facet_wrap(~ offered_mps, labeller = label_both) +
labs(x = "Worst-end CPU steal during the repetition (%)",
y = "Delivered % of offered load", colour = "Protocol", shape = "Provider",
title = "Contention against delivery, intra-AZ, one point per repetition",
subtitle = "Placement fixed and rate faceted. TCP sits at 100% throughout; UDP falls as steal rises.") +
theme_bw()
plot(output); dev.off(); to_svg() # output to the html page

sql_code: -- Where STACKIT appears to have a latency cliff and the others do not: asking
-- for 5x the bitrate returned roughly the same packet rate, around 60k/s,
-- while AWS and GCP went faster when pushed harder.
-- Read this with "Hypervisor CPU steal, and which rows it invalidates" and
-- "How contention moves tail latency", both in the Data Quality group (this
-- query is in Capacity). The ceiling was not
-- a NIC or provider packet-rate limit. It was CPU steal on the hypervisor:
-- across 53 STACKIT repetitions at the 100k rung, worst-end steal correlated
-- at r = -0.97 with delivered message rate -- uncontended hosts delivered
-- 73.9k-92.9k msg/s, contended ones 37.7k-47.8k. On an uncontended host STACKIT
-- reaches ~93% of a 100k msg/s offered load, so there is no 60k ceiling to
-- explain.
-- Three guest-side explanations were tested directly and all three are
-- negative. netdev_budget 300 -> 1000 (confirmed applied via the read-back)
-- changed nothing, because softnet_stat time_squeeze is already 0.6 per
-- million packets on an uncontended host -- the budget was never the binding
-- constraint. busy_poll changed nothing once steal was matched. An RPS mask
-- steering receive work to another core (confirmed by received_rps) made
-- latency 1.4-2.1x worse below 25k msg/s, the handoff costing more than the
-- contention it relieved.
-- time_squeeze does rise on contended hosts -- 0.6 per million packets below
-- 3% steal, 266 above 25% -- but that is a stolen time slice ending a poll
-- with work still queued, not an exhausted budget. Same counter, different
-- cause.
-- What this query cannot answer: whether placement changes delivered rate.
-- Each AWS and GCP placement rests on a single provisioning, so placement is
-- confounded with which VM pair and path were drawn. The orderings are
-- non-monotonic and contradict each other between providers -- at 5 Gbit AWS
-- runs different-host 187k > cross-region 140k > multi-az 124k while GCP runs
-- cross-region 196k > multi-az 171k > different-host 141k -- and GCP's order
-- inverts between the 1 and 5 Gbit targets on the same VMs. Distance costs
-- latency, not delivery: UDP has no feedback loop, so a longer path drops
-- nothing by itself. Loss here runs 26-68% in every condition including
-- intra-AZ, while both hosts sit at 55-60% idle with zero steal, so it is
-- endpoint shaping rather than the path. Treat these as a per-provisioning
-- capacity envelope, not a placement comparison.
SELECT provider,
placement_class,
benchmark_name,
udp_target_bitrate_gbit_per_sec           AS target_gbit_s,
round(median(receiver_mbit_per_sec))      AS delivered_mbit_s,
round(median(approx_packets_per_sec))     AS packets_per_sec,
round(median(lost_percent), 2)            AS loss_pct,
-- Contention, on the same row as the numbers it may explain. NULL means
-- the run has no CPU telemetry, not that the host was quiet.
round(avg(worst_steal_pct), 1)            AS steal_pct
FROM network_capacity
WHERE protocol = 'udp'
-- Standard tuning only. STACKIT is the one provider that also ran a tuned
-- arm, so pooling the two would mix treatments -- and those runs happened to
-- draw quieter hosts, which biases pooled STACKIT figures optimistically:
-- at 100k UDP the tuned rows read 81.3% delivered against standard's 44.1%.
AND os_tuning = 'standard'
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3, 4
ORDER BY 1, 2, 4
r_code: to_svg <- svgstring(width = output.width.inch, height = output.height.inch, scaling = 1)
### the current table is bound to the variable 'df'
output <- ggplot(df, aes(x = factor(target_gbit_s), y = packets_per_sec, fill = provider)) +
geom_col(position = "dodge") +
facet_wrap(~ placement_class) +
scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
labs(x = "Offered bitrate (Gbit/s)", y = "Delivered packets/s", fill = "Provider") +
theme_bw()

description: Do burst credits decay during a capacity run?
sql_code: -- AWS c6id.large is a burst-credited instance ("Up to 12.5 Gbps"), so a capacity
-- figure could be peak-then-baseline rather than sustained. Credit depletion
-- shows as a downward slope across the run; a flat trace means the number is a
-- cap being saturated, at least at this duration.
SELECT provider,
round(interval_start_sec)            AS second,
round(median(mbit_per_sec))          AS mbit_s
FROM network_capacity_intervals
WHERE protocol = 'tcp'
-- Standard tuning only. STACKIT is the one provider that also ran a tuned
-- arm, so pooling the two would mix treatments -- and those runs happened to
-- draw quieter hosts, which biases pooled STACKIT figures optimistically:
-- at 100k UDP the tuned rows read 81.3% delivered against standard's 44.1%.
AND os_tuning = 'standard'
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2

### the current table is bound to the variable 'df'
output <- ggplot(df, aes(x = second, y = mbit_s, colour = provider)) +
geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
labs(x = "Second within the 15s run", y = "Throughput (Mbit/s)", colour = "Provider") +

sql_code: -- Ping-pong is closed-loop: it sends, waits for the reply, then sends again. When
-- the system stalls it simply issues fewer requests, so it stops sampling exactly
-- when it should be measuring. Under-load keeps to a schedule regardless, so the
-- stalls land in the histogram. A lower ping-pong tail is not a better result.
SELECT provider,
placement_class,
protocol,
round(median(CASE WHEN mode = 'pp' THEN p50_rtt_us END), 1)                        AS pingpong_p50_us,
round(median(CASE WHEN mode = 'ul' AND offered_mps = 1000 THEN p50_rtt_us END), 1) AS underload_1k_p50_us,
round(median(CASE WHEN mode = 'pp' THEN p99_rtt_us END), 1)                        AS pingpong_p99_us,
round(median(CASE WHEN mode = 'ul' AND offered_mps = 1000 THEN p99_rtt_us END), 1) AS underload_1k_p99_us,
-- Contention, on the same row as the numbers it may explain. NULL means
-- the run has no CPU telemetry, not that the host was quiet.
round(avg(worst_steal_pct), 1)            AS steal_pct
FROM network_latency
-- Standard tuning only. STACKIT is the one provider that also ran a tuned
-- arm, so pooling the two would mix treatments -- and those runs happened to
-- draw quieter hosts, which biases pooled STACKIT figures optimistically:
-- at 100k UDP the tuned rows read 81.3% delivered against standard's 44.1%.
WHERE os_tuning = 'standard'
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
ORDER BY 1, 2, 3

description: Was the ladder ever bandwidth limited?
sql_code: -- Standard tuning only throughout, in both CTEs: STACKIT also ran a tuned arm.
-- No: the ladder peaks around 100 Mbit/s while the same pair carries 8-10 Gbit/s
-- over TCP. Every ceiling this study found was packet-rate or endpoint bound.
-- Without this arm that claim would be an inference rather than a measurement.
WITH ladder AS (
SELECT provider, placement_class,
round(max(delivered_mps) * 64 * 2 * 8 / 1e6, 1) AS ladder_peak_mbit_s,
round(max(packets_per_sec))                     AS ladder_peak_pps
FROM network_latency
WHERE mode = 'ul'
AND os_tuning = 'standard'
GROUP BY 1, 2
capacity AS (
SELECT provider, placement_class,
round(median(receiver_mbit_per_sec)) AS tcp_capacity_mbit_s
FROM network_capacity
WHERE protocol = 'tcp'
AND os_tuning = 'standard'
GROUP BY 1, 2
SELECT l.provider, l.placement_class,
l.ladder_peak_mbit_s, l.ladder_peak_pps, c.tcp_capacity_mbit_s,
round(100.0 * l.ladder_peak_mbit_s / nullif(c.tcp_capacity_mbit_s, 0), 2) AS ladder_pct_of_capacity
FROM ladder l
JOIN capacity c USING (provider, placement_class)
ORDER BY 1, 2
